**Data** is simply recorded facts. The number of bottles of zobo you sold on Saturday is data. So is the name of the customer who paid by transfer, the date a cooperative member made her contribution, and the comment a client left on your WhatsApp status. When facts are written down in an organised way, you can count them, compare them and learn from them. When they stay in your head, they turn into guesses.

**Data literacy** is the ability to read, work with, question and talk about data. It does not mean advanced mathematics. It means you can look at a sales record, a chart in a newspaper or a donor report and ask: what does this really show, is it accurate, and what should I do about it?

Numbers come in two kinds. **Counts** are whole numbers, such as 3 customers or 12 tubers of yam. **Measurements** can have parts, such as 1.5 litres or 2.75 kg. Categories are not numbers even when they look like them: a member ID like 0457 is a label, so it makes no sense to add member IDs together.
Where your data comes from
**Records you already keep:** a sales notebook, receipts, a cooperative contribution register, attendance lists.
**Digital traces:** your bank or Opay and Moniepoint transaction history, POS slips, WhatsApp Business catalogue views, Paystack payment reports.
**Data you collect on purpose:** a short survey on Google Forms, a tally sheet at a market stall, a phone call to past customers.
**Data other people publish:** for example, the National Bureau of Statistics publishes inflation and price reports you can read online.

The first three are **primary data**: you collected it yourself for your own purpose. The last is **secondary data**: someone else collected it. Secondary data can save time, but you must check who made it, when and how.
Start with a question, not a spreadsheet

Many people start by collecting everything and end up with a notebook full of numbers they never use. Good analysts start with a clear question. A vague worry such as "business is slow" becomes useful when you sharpen it: "Which days of the week bring the most sales?" or "Did more customers pay by transfer in September than in August?" A good question names what you will measure and over what period.

Worked example: which day should she make extra zobo?
For example, Amaka sells chilled zobo near a bus park in Ibadan. She feels Saturdays are busy but often throws away unsold bottles on other days. She records sales for one week.
Her question: "How many bottles do I sell on each day of the week?"
She writes a tally each evening: Mon 18, Tue 15, Wed 17, Thu 16, Fri 26, Sat 34, Sun 12.
She adds them: 18 + 15 + 17 + 16 + 26 + 34 + 12 = 138 bottles for the week.
She finds the average per day: 138 ÷ 7 = about 19.7 bottles.
She compares: Friday (26) and Saturday (34) are well above average; Sunday (12) is well below.
Amaka decides to make about 20 bottles on weekdays, about 30 on Friday, 35 on Saturday and only 12 on Sunday, and to keep recording for three more weeks to check the pattern holds.
One week is a start, not a proof
A single week can be unusual because of rain, a public holiday or a church event. Collect at least three or four weeks before making a big change, such as buying more stock on credit.
Data, information and insight

It helps to separate three ideas. **Data** is the raw record: 34 bottles on Saturday. **Information** is data organised so it means something: Saturday sells almost three times as much as Sunday. **Insight** is what you understand and act on: make more on Saturday, less on Sunday, and stop wasting stock. Your aim in every task is to move from data to insight.

Notice what happened in the example. Amaka did not need any app. She needed a clear question, honest daily records and simple arithmetic. In the rest of this course you will do the same steps faster and more accurately in a spreadsheet, and you will learn to present the result so others trust it.

Data people use a few words again and again. Once you know them, spreadsheets, reports and charts become much easier to read. This lesson covers the words for the parts of a table and the five calculations you will use most.
The parts of a data table
**Dataset:** the whole collection of records about one topic, for example all sales in September.
**Record (row):** one item or event, such as one sale or one member. Each row is one record.
**Variable (column):** one thing you measure about every record, such as date, item, quantity or amount.
**Value:** a single entry, such as "Rice" or 2,500.
**Cell:** the box where a row and column meet. In a spreadsheet, cell B4 is column B, row 4.
A table of data with rows and columns
Each row is one record and each column is one variable; keeping this rule makes every calculation easier.

Spreadsheets also care about **data types**. A cell can hold a number, text, a date or a formula. If you type "2k" instead of 2000, the spreadsheet sees text and will leave it out of totals. Typing amounts as plain numbers, without the naira sign or words, keeps every calculation correct. You can add the ₦ sign later with formatting.

Worked example: what does a typical customer spend?

For example, Halima runs a small provisions kiosk in Kaduna. On Tuesday morning she records what seven customers spent, in naira: 1,500; 2,000; 2,000; 2,500; 3,000; 3,500; 20,000. The 20,000 was a caterer buying in bulk.

The median of ₦2,500 is the better answer to "what does a typical customer spend?" because one bulk buyer pulled the mean far upwards.

Percentages and percentage change

A **percentage** compares a part with a whole. If 18 of your 60 customers paid by POS, that is 18 ÷ 60 × 100 = 30%. Percentages let you compare groups of different sizes fairly: 30 transfers out of 50 sales (60%) is a bigger share than 40 transfers out of 100 sales (40%), even though 40 is the larger number.

A **percentage change** tells you how much something grew or fell compared with where it started. The formula is: (new value minus old value) ÷ old value × 100. If sales were ₦250,000 in August and ₦300,000 in September, the change is (300,000 minus 250,000) ÷ 250,000 × 100 = 20% growth. Always divide by the **old** value, not the new one. Dividing by the new value here would give about 16.7%, which is wrong.
Percentage points are not percent

If the share of customers paying by transfer moves from 40% to 50%, it rose by 10 percentage points, but by 25% in relative terms (10 ÷ 40 × 100). Reports sometimes mix these up, so check which one is meant.
Worked example: comparing two weeks fairly
For example, Halima wants to know whether more of her customers are paying by transfer. In week 1 she had 50 sales and 30 were transfers. In week 2 she had 80 sales and 40 were transfers.
Week 1 share: 30 ÷ 50 × 100 = 60% transfers.
Week 2 share: 40 ÷ 80 × 100 = 50% transfers.
Change in share: 50% minus 60% = a fall of 10 percentage points.
Change in number of transfers: (40 minus 30) ÷ 30 × 100 = about 33% more transfers.
Both statements are true: she received more transfers in week 2, but transfers made up a smaller share of her sales because cash sales grew faster. A careful report says both.
Rates and ratios

A **rate** is a count over a period or per group, for example 12 new members per month, or 3 complaints per 100 orders. A **ratio** compares two amounts, for example 2 cash payments for every 5 transfers, written 2:5. Rates per 100 or per 1,000 let you compare a small group with a big one.

Saving data bundles

Spreadsheets with text and numbers are small files. Most data is used when you first install the app and when you open charts or many images. Do heavier work on Wi-Fi when you can, and keep files focused rather than adding photos inside them.
Protecting your account and files
Use a strong, unique password for your Google account: a long phrase is easier to remember and harder to guess than a short word with numbers.
Turn on **2-Step Verification** in your Google account security settings, so a stolen password alone cannot open your files.
When you share a file, choose the right level: **Viewer** can only look, **Commenter** can suggest, **Editor** can change everything. Give Editor only to people who truly need it.
Avoid "Anyone with the link" for files that contain names, phone numbers or money records.
Use **File, Version history** to see and restore earlier versions if someone deletes or changes data by mistake.
Data about other people is a responsibility

Customer phone numbers, member contributions and addresses are **personal data**. Nigeria has a law about this: the **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023**, enforced by the **Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC)**. For a small business or community group, the practical lessons are simple: collect only what you need, tell people why you are collecting it, keep it secure, use it only for that purpose, and do not pass it to others without permission.

The Act also gives people rights over their own data, such as the right to know what you hold about them and to ask for it to be corrected. In practice, that means keeping records tidy enough that you can find one person's entries quickly, and correcting mistakes when a member or customer points them out. If you ever handle data for a larger organisation, ask whether it has a data protection policy and follow it.

Most spreadsheet problems start with layout, not formulas. If the table is arranged well, every calculation in this course takes seconds. If it is messy, even simple totals go wrong. This lesson shows you the layout that analysts call **tidy data**, then the first five formulas you will use every week.
The tidy data rules
**One row per record.** Each sale, member payment or order gets its own row.
**One column per variable.** Date in one column, item in another, quantity in another. Do not write "3 bags rice" in one cell; split it into Quantity: 3 and Item: Rice.
**One header row at the top.** Short, clear headings in row 1, such as Date, Item, Qty, Unit price, Amount, Payment.
**No merged cells, no blank rows, no totals in the middle.** Keep totals in a separate area or a summary sheet.
**Consistent values.** Always write "Rice", not sometimes "rice" or "Rice (50kg)". Always enter dates the same way.

Why does this matter so much? Because a spreadsheet only understands what is in each cell. If one cell says "3 bags rice", the spreadsheet cannot multiply it, count it as rice or add it to a total. Splitting facts into their own columns is a few extra taps when you enter data, and it saves hours later.
How formulas work

A **formula** always starts with an equals sign (=). It can use numbers, cell references and functions. A **cell reference** like D2 means "whatever is in cell D2". If the value in D2 changes, every formula that uses D2 updates by itself. A **range** like E2:E31 means all the cells from E2 down to E31. A **function** is a ready-made calculation, such as SUM or AVERAGE.

Filling a formula down a column

You do not need to type the Amount formula in every row. Type =C2*D2 in cell E2. On a computer, drag the small square at the bottom right of the cell (the **fill handle**) down the column. **Freeze the header row** (on a computer: View, Freeze, 1 row; on the phone: tap the row number, then Freeze) so the headings stay visible as you scroll down.

A month of sales might be 200 or 300 rows. Nobody can see a pattern by scrolling through that many lines. The skill in this lesson is **summarising**: turning many rows into a short table that answers a question, such as "Which items bring in the most money?" or "How do most customers pay?"
Two functions that summarise by category

**SUMIF** adds up only the rows that match a condition. Its pattern is =SUMIF(range to check, what to look for, range to add). For example, =SUMIF(B2:B300,"Rice",E2:E300) looks down column B for the word Rice and adds the matching amounts from column E.

**COUNTIF** counts the rows that match a condition. Its pattern is =COUNTIF(range to check, what to look for). For example, =COUNTIF(F2:F300,"Transfer") counts how many sales were paid by transfer. Instead of typing "Rice" inside the formula, you can point to a cell that contains the word, such as =SUMIF(B$2:B$300,H2,E$2:E$300). The $ signs lock the range so it does not move when you copy the formula down.

Worked example: where does the money come from?
For example, Ada runs a provisions shop in Abeokuta. Her September log has 220 sales worth ₦400,000 in total. She builds a summary sheet with each item in column H and SUMIF formulas next to them.
SUMIF results by item: Rice ₦180,000; Beans ₦72,000; Palm oil ₦60,000; Garri ₦48,000; Others ₦40,000. Check: these add to ₦400,000, the same as =SUM of all amounts.
Share of total: Rice 180,000 ÷ 400,000 × 100 = 45%; Beans 18%; Palm oil 15%; Garri 12%; Others 10%. Check: the shares add to 100%.
COUNTIF by payment method: Transfer 120, Cash 70, POS 30. Check: 120 + 70 + 30 = 220 sales.
Payment shares: Transfer 120 ÷ 220 × 100 = about 54.5%; Cash about 31.8%; POS about 13.6%.
Average sale: ₦400,000 ÷ 220 = about ₦1,818.

Rice alone brings in almost half of her sales, so running out of rice is her biggest risk; she decides to keep a minimum of two bags in stock. More than half of payments are transfers, so she prints her account details clearly at the counter and checks every alert in her bank app before releasing goods.

Always check your summary adds up

A summary is only trustworthy if it agrees with the raw data. After any SUMIF table, add the category totals and compare them with =SUM of the whole amount column. If they differ, some rows have a category spelled differently ("rice" with a space, for instance) or left blank. Fixing those is the subject of Module 3, Lesson 1.

You can also count with two conditions at once using **COUNTIFS** and **SUMIFS**. For example, =SUMIFS(E2:E300,B2:B300,"Rice",F2:F300,"POS") adds only the rice sales paid by POS. Notice that in SUMIFS the range to add comes first, the opposite of SUMIF. When a formula gives a strange result, check the order of its parts first.
Sorting and filtering

**Sort** puts rows in order. Select the whole table first, not just one column, otherwise the amounts get separated from their items. Sorting by Amount from largest to smallest shows your biggest sales at the top.

**Filter** hides rows you do not need for now without deleting them. In the browser version, choose Data, Create a filter, then tap the filter icon on a heading, for example to show only POS payments or only one week.
**Filter views** (browser version) let you save a filter without changing what other people see in a shared sheet.
Pivot tables, when you are ready

A pivot table builds a summary like Ada's automatically. In the browser version of Google Sheets, select your table and choose Insert, Pivot table, then add Item as Rows and Amount as Values (SUM). Learn SUMIF first so you understand what the pivot table is doing.

Common chart mistakes to avoid
**Too many slices in a pie.** Above about five slices, group the small ones into "Others" or switch to a bar chart.

**Charting the wrong measure.** If customer numbers changed a lot, the share of sales may tell a fairer story than raw totals.

Tools for each problem

**Extra spaces:** in a new column, type =TRIM(B2) and copy it down. TRIM removes spaces at the start and end and turns double spaces into single ones. In the browser version, Data, Data cleanup, Trim whitespace does the same in place.
**Inconsistent capital letters:** =PROPER(B2) turns "jos north" into "Jos North". You can combine them: =PROPER(TRIM(B2)).

**Duplicates:** in the browser version, select the table and choose Data, Data cleanup, Remove duplicates. To check before deleting, add a helper column with =COUNTIF(A$2:A$200,A2)>1, which shows TRUE for any value that appears more than once.
**Blanks:** =COUNTBLANK(E2:E200) tells you how many empty cells there are; use a filter to show only blanks and fill them from your notebook or receipts.
**Text numbers:** retype them as plain numbers, or use =VALUE(E2) for numbers stored as text.
**Typos and extremes:** use =MAX and =MIN on each numeric column. If the largest contribution is ₦500,000 in a group where most pay ₦5,000, check that row against the original record.

After cleaning a column with a formula, copy the clean column and use **Paste special, Values only** to replace the original. Otherwise the clean column still depends on the messy one, and deleting the messy one breaks it.
Worked example: cleaning a cooperative contribution list

For example, Grace is the new financial secretary of a cooperative in Jos with three branches. She receives a 60-row contribution list for September compiled from three branch WhatsApp reports. The SUM of the Amount column is ₦612,000.
She applies =PROPER(TRIM()) to the Branch column. Five different spellings collapse into the three correct branch names.
A COUNTIF helper column on Receipt number flags 3 rows as TRUE. Each is a ₦5,000 payment posted by two branch secretaries. She deletes the extra copies: 3 × 5,000 = ₦15,000 removed.
=COUNTBLANK shows 2 empty Amount cells. She checks the receipts: both members paid ₦5,000, so she fills them in. The total rises by ₦10,000.
=MAX shows one entry of ₦50,000. The receipt says ₦5,000; she corrects it, reducing the total by ₦45,000.
New total: 612,000 minus 15,000 plus 10,000 minus 45,000 = ₦562,000, and it now matches the bank statement.

The cleaned list has 57 rows, three correct branch names and a total that agrees with the bank. Grace records each change in a short cleaning log so the executive can see exactly what was corrected and why.

Honest analysis: privacy, bias and misleading claims
Anonymise personal data before sharing it
Spot sampling bias and low response rates in surveys
Explain why correlation does not prove causation
Recognise misleading charts and numbers, and avoid making them

Data can be accurate and still be used badly. It can expose people's private details, leave out the people who most need to be counted, or be presented in a way that pushes the reader to a wrong conclusion. Ethical data work protects people and tells the truth, even when the truth is less exciting.
Protect people first
**Collect the minimum.** If you only need to know how many women attended, you do not need their home addresses.
**Anonymise before sharing.** Replace names with codes (P01, P02) and remove phone numbers when sending a report to a donor, a WhatsApp group or a partner.
**Watch small groups.** If only one widow in a village group received support, reporting "1 widow in Ward 3" may identify her. Combine small groups or report them more broadly.
**Ask for consent.** On a survey, state at the top what the answers are for and who will see them, and make sensitive questions optional.
A personal profile card with protected details
Before any report leaves your phone, check that no one can be identified who did not agree to it.

Screenshots are a frequent leak. A screenshot of a member list or payment record posted in a large WhatsApp group can be forwarded anywhere within minutes. Share a summary instead, or a version with codes in place of names.
Who is missing from the data?

**Bias** in data means the data leans one way and does not fairly represent the group you care about. A common cause is **sampling bias**: the people who answered are not like the people who did not. A survey shared only by WhatsApp link misses members without smartphones or data. A survey at a Saturday market misses women who work on Saturdays. Always ask: who was able to respond, and who was not?

Also look at the **response rate**: responses ÷ people asked × 100. A low response rate does not make results useless, but it means you should describe them as "of those who replied" rather than "members say".
Worked example: a survey that needs care

For example, the coordinator of a women's group in Enugu with 120 members sends a Google Forms link on WhatsApp asking which day members prefer for training. She receives 48 responses, and 36 choose Saturday.
Response rate: 48 ÷ 120 × 100 = 40%.
Among respondents: 36 ÷ 48 × 100 = 75% prefer Saturday.
She notices that almost no older members responded; many of them use basic phones without data.
She asks branch leaders to collect answers from non-respondents by phone call or at the next meeting, using the same question.
She reports: "75% of the 48 members who replied online prefer Saturday; we are collecting answers from the other members before deciding."
Instead of claiming "75% of members want Saturday", she gives an honest picture and fills the gap, so the final decision reflects the whole group, not only those with smartphones.
Correlation versus causation
Correlation
Causation
Two things move together
Seen in the data
May share a hidden cause
One thing makes the other happen
Needs stronger evidence
Tested by changing one thing
Two numbers rising together is a clue to investigate, not proof that one causes the other.
Correlation is not causation

If zobo sales and electric fan sales both rise from February to April, they are **correlated**: they move together. Zobo does not cause fan sales. Both are driven by a third factor, hot weather. When you see two measures move together, ask whether something else could explain both before concluding one causes the other. The fairest way to test a cause in a small business is to change one thing at a time, for example to run a price discount for two weeks while keeping everything else the same, and compare with similar weeks.
Misleading numbers and charts
**Cut-off axes** that make a small change look dramatic.
**Cherry-picked periods**, such as showing only the three best months.
**Big percentages from tiny numbers**: "sales up 100%" may mean from 2 to 4 orders.
**Averages that hide spread**: an average profit of ₦50,000 a month across members may hide that most earn far less.

**Investment schemes that show steady high returns.** Promises of fixed, high monthly returns, with charts and screenshots as "proof", are a classic warning sign of Ponzi schemes. Check any investment platform's registration with the Securities and Exchange Commission Nigeria before paying.
Your own honesty checklist

Before you send a report, read each claim and ask three questions. How many records or people is this based on? Over what period? What would someone who disagrees point out? If a finding only holds for one good week, say so. If a chart starts its axis above zero, either fix it or label it clearly. Reporting a disappointing result honestly builds more trust with a donor, an employer or your group than a polished but misleading one, and it helps you make better decisions yourself.

Worked example: September results for a provisions shop
For example, Ada (from Module 2) wants to know if her September sales of ₦400,000 were profitable. She checks her purchase receipts and expenses. All figures are illustrative.
Revenue: ₦400,000 from 220 sales.
Cost of goods sold: ₦290,000. Gross profit: 400,000 minus 290,000 = ₦110,000.
Running costs: ₦20,000 for transport, phone data and her share of shop rent. Net profit: 110,000 minus 20,000 = ₦90,000, a net margin of 22.5%.
Average order value: 400,000 ÷ 220 = about ₦1,818.
Customers: she can identify 64 regular customers from transfer names and her notebook; 40 bought more than once. Repeat rate: 40 ÷ 64 × 100 = 62.5%.

Ada now knows that of every ₦100 she sells, about ₦27.50 is gross profit and about ₦22.50 is left after running costs. If her supplier raises prices and she does not adjust her selling prices, she will see it first in a falling gross margin.
Break-even: how much must you sell?

Your **break-even point** is the level of sales where you cover all your costs and make neither profit nor loss. For a single product the formula is: fixed costs ÷ (selling price minus cost per unit). The amount left from each sale after paying for the item itself is called the **contribution**.

For example, suppose a trader's fixed costs are ₦20,000 a month (stall fee, data, transport) and she sells a paint bucket of garri for ₦2,500 that cost her ₦2,000. Each bucket contributes ₦500. Break-even = 20,000 ÷ 500 = 40 buckets a month. Every bucket after the 40th adds ₦500 profit. If her supplier raises the cost to ₦2,200, the contribution falls to ₦300 and she needs about 67 buckets to break even, which shows why tracking costs matters as much as tracking sales.

Analysis only creates value when someone understands it and acts. A busy manager, a donor or a cooperative meeting will not read your spreadsheet. They need the answer, the key evidence and what you want them to do, in that order. This lesson shows you how to present data for different audiences.
Know your audience
Audience
What they care about
What to show
Client or customer
Reliability, value, results for them
Delivery record, satisfaction, before-and-after results
Employer or manager

Donor or funder

Totals, who benefited, what happens next
Lead with the answer

Many reports tell the story in the order the work was done: we collected data, then cleaned it, then calculated. Readers prefer the opposite. Start with your main message in one sentence, then give two or three supporting numbers, then one chart, then your recommendation. Put the method and detailed tables at the end or in an attachment for those who want to check.
The one-page report structure
Main message first
Two or three numbers
One clear chart
What it means
What we should do
This order respects the reader's time and makes the action impossible to miss.
A woman presenting a chart to an audience
Lead with the answer and support it with a few numbers and one honest chart.
Presenting in a meeting
**Open with the question and the answer** in under a minute: "We asked why deliveries were late. The main reason is group orders."
**Show one chart at a time** and say what to look at: "Look at the September bar, it is the tallest."
**Read numbers slowly and round them.** Say "about one in eight orders" rather than "11.9 percent" when speaking.
**Stop and ask for questions** before giving the recommendation, so people feel heard.
**Close with the decision you need** and who will do what by when.

If you present on a phone or in a group video call, prepare the chart as a single clear image beforehand. Large text and a short message title matter even more on a small screen, and many participants may join with weak connections.
Outputs and outcomes

Donors and development partners often ask for both. **Outputs** are what you delivered: 45 women trained, 6 sessions held. **Outcomes** are the changes that followed: how many women started using the skill, earned more or kept records. Outcomes are harder to measure but matter more. Measure them with a simple follow-up, such as a phone call or form one or three months later, and report how many people you were able to reach.
Worked example: one set of results, two messages

For example, a community skills programme in Ilorin trained women in bookkeeping. Of 45 enrolled, 38 completed. In a three-month follow-up by phone, the coordinator reached all 38, and 25 said they now keep weekly sales records.
Completion rate: 38 ÷ 45 × 100 = about 84.4%.
Outcome rate: 25 ÷ 38 × 100 = about 65.8% of completers keep weekly records.

Donor report headline: "Two in three graduates now keep weekly sales records three months after training." She adds the numbers, a bar chart of enrolled, completed and keeping records, the main reason 7 women did not finish (clashes with market days) and a request to fund a Saturday cohort.

WhatsApp message to members: "Thank you all! 38 of us finished the course and 25 now keep weekly records. Next cohort will meet on Saturdays so market women can join. Reply YES if you want to help mentor."
The same data serves both audiences. The donor sees honest outputs, outcomes and a clear funding request; members see their achievement and a concrete next step.

Notice that the donor version includes the 7 women who did not finish and the reason why. Leaving out disappointing numbers is tempting, but funders usually notice, and the reason for dropping out is exactly what helps design a better programme.
Writing a short data message
**One message per update.** Do not pack five findings into one WhatsApp message.
**Use real numbers, rounded sensibly.** "About 2 in 3" or "66%" is easier to read than 65.79%.
**Compare with something.** "₦315,000 in September, up from ₦260,000 in August" means more than one number alone.
**End with an action or question.** What do you want the reader to do?
**Attach the chart as an image**, not the whole spreadsheet, unless they need to check the details.
Be ready for the hard question

Expect someone to ask "How do you know?" Keep your workbook and data dictionary ready, and be honest about limits, such as a small sample or a follow-up that did not reach everyone. Admitting limits usually increases trust.
Different audiences need the same truth framed for what they care about.

A weekly data habit

Skills fade if they are not used. The simplest way to keep them is a short weekly routine at a fixed time, for example Sunday evening or Monday morning. Thirty minutes is enough for a small business or group.
Enter or check the week's records and fix any errors (10 minutes).
Look at your dashboard: are your 3 to 5 KPIs on target? (5 minutes)
Look for one surprise: the highest or lowest number, or a change from last week (5 minutes).
Write one decision for the coming week (5 minutes).
Once a month, do a longer review with a chart and share a short summary with your partner, team or group.
Worked example: a 90-day plan

For example, Halima (from Module 1) finishes the course and wants to grow her kiosk. Today her average weekly revenue is about ₦95,000, her gross margin is about 24% and she has no record of repeat customers.
Days 1 to 30: record every sale in Google Sheets with a dropdown for item and payment method; set up a dashboard with weekly revenue, gross margin and stock-outs.
Days 31 to 60: start a simple customer list (with permission) to measure repeat customers; review supplier prices and aim to raise gross margin from 24% to 26%.
Days 61 to 90: use the data to test one change, such as a small bulk-buy discount for two weeks, and compare with the two weeks before.
Targets for day 90: 12 weeks of complete records, gross margin at least 26%, a repeat customer rate measured for the first time, and one tested change with a written result.
Her plan is specific, measurable and based on her own data. At day 90 she can show, with numbers, what changed and what she learned.
Making targets measurable

A target is useful only if, at the end of the period, you can say clearly whether you met it. "Grow my business" cannot be checked. "Raise gross margin from 24% to 26% by the end of December" can. Each target should name the metric, the starting point, the goal and the date. Keep the number of targets small, three is plenty, so that you actually track them every week.

Keep customers
Measure repeat customer rate monthly and reach 50% by day 90
Fewer complaints
Cut late deliveries from about 12% to under 5% next quarter

Some weeks will go badly: a power cut wipes out a day of trade, or you forget to record sales during a busy festive week. That is normal. Note what happened in your log, fill in what you can from bank alerts and receipts, and continue. A record with a few honest gaps is far more useful than no record at all.

Why this matters
Data is simply recorded facts
Written facts can be counted and compared
Facts in your head turn into guesses
Data literacy: read, question and talk about data
No advanced mathematics needed
Data is simply recorded facts. The bottles of zobo you sold on Saturday, or the date a member paid her contribution.
When facts are written down in an organised way, you can count them, compare them and learn from them.
When they stay in your head, they turn into guesses.
Data literacy means you can look at a sales record or a chart and ask: what does this really show, is it accurate, and what should I do? It does not need advanced mathematics.
Know your data
Four kinds of data
Numbers: amounts you can add or average
Categories: labels like cash, transfer, POS
Dates and times: when something happened
Free text: words people write or say
Numbers, like bottles sold or amount paid, can be added and averaged.
Categories can only be counted. A member ID like 0457 is a label, so it makes no sense to add member IDs together.
Dates let you group by day, week or month and see trends.
And free text, like the bottle was not cold enough, is read for themes and repeated complaints.
Worked example
Which day needs extra zobo?
Start with a clear question, not a spreadsheet.
Ask: how many bottles do I sell each day?
Collect: a tally every evening
Organise: add up the week, 138 bottles
Analyse: average about 19.7 a day
Decide: make more Friday and Saturday
For example, Amaka sells chilled zobo near a bus park in Ibadan, and often throws away unsold bottles. Business is slow is a worry. A good question names what you measure and when.
She writes a tally each evening for one week: 18, 15, 17, 16, then 26 on Friday, 34 on Saturday and 12 on Sunday. That is 138 bottles.
138 divided by 7 is about 19.7 bottles a day. Friday and Saturday are well above that, and Sunday is well below.
So she makes about 30 on Friday, 35 on Saturday and only 12 on Sunday.
But one week can be unusual because of rain or a holiday, so she keeps recording for three more weeks before any big change.
What does a typical customer spend?
Add all 7 amounts, 34,500 naira, and divide by 7. One bulk buyer pulls it up.
Sort the amounts and take the middle one. This is the typical customer.
The amount that appears most often. Range: 20,000 minus 1,500 is ₦18,500.
For example, Halima runs a provisions kiosk in Kaduna. Seven customers spend between 1,500 and 3,500 naira, plus one caterer who spends 20,000.
The mean adds everything and divides by 7. That gives about 4,929 naira, but only one customer spent more than that.
The median is the middle value once they are sorted: 2,500 naira. That is the better answer, because one bulk buyer pulled the mean far upwards.
The mode is the most common value, 2,000. The range shows how spread out the values are.
Choose well
Use the mean when the values are fairly similar.
When one or two values are extreme, as with incomes, prices and rents, report the median.
Percentage change
Did sales really grow?
For example, a business compares its sales in August and September.
Sales in August (old)
Sales in September (new)
Always divide by the old value.
A percentage compares a part with a whole: part divided by whole, times 100. Percentage change is new minus old, divided by old, times 100.
Sales were 250,000 naira in August and 300,000 in September. The change is 50,000 divided by 250,000, times 100. That is 20% growth.
The common mistake is dividing by the new value. That gives about 16.7%, which is wrong.

Choose and read charts correctly
Most spreadsheet problems start with layout, not formulas. If the table is arranged well, every calculation takes seconds.
Then you let formulas do the adding, and turn a whole month of rows into a short table that answers a question.
Finally you choose a chart that matches your question, and label it honestly.
Step by step
One row per record. One column per variable.
One row for each sale, payment or order
One column for each fact: date, item, qty
One header row at the top
No merged cells, blank rows or mid totals
Same spelling and date style every time
Each sale gets its own row. And each fact gets its own column. Do not write 3 bags rice in one cell. Split it into Quantity 3 and Item Rice.
Put short, clear headings in row 1, such as Date, Item, Qty, Unit price, Amount and Payment.
Keep totals in a separate area. Always write Rice the same way, and type amounts as plain numbers, without the naira sign or k. Text is left out of totals.
First formulas
Formulas that do the work
=C2*D2 multiplies quantity by unit price
=SUM(E2:E31) adds every amount
=AVERAGE and =MEDIAN for a typical sale
=COUNT counts the sales recorded
=MAX and =MIN find biggest and smallest
Every formula starts with an equals sign. For example, Chioma sells foodstuff in Onitsha main market. Garri: 6 buckets at 2,500 naira. Her formula, C4 times D4, gives 15,000.
She copies the formula down the column, and each row adjusts by itself.
SUM adds a whole range of cells, from top to bottom.
AVERAGE, MEDIAN, COUNT, MAX and MIN answer most first questions.
Every time Chioma adds a sale, her totals update. No more adding up the notebook at night, and no arithmetic slips.
Worked example
Where does Ada's money come from?
For example, Ada's provisions shop in Abeokuta made 220 sales in September.
Rice
Beans
Palm oil
Garri
Others
Totals by item using SUMIF.
A month can have hundreds of rows. Nobody sees a pattern by scrolling. SUMIF adds up only the rows that match a condition, such as the word Rice.
Ada lists each item and uses SUMIF beside it. Rice brings in 180,000 naira. That is 180,000 divided by 400,000, times 100, which is 45%.
Her items add up to 400,000, the same as the SUM of every amount, and her shares add to 100%. Always run this check. If it does not match, some rows are spelled differently.
Rice is almost half her sales, so she keeps at least two bags in stock.
Summarising
Count, add, then check
Counts rows that match. Ada: 120 transfers, 70 cash, 30 POS, which is 220 sales.
Category divided by total, times 100. Transfers are about 54.5% of Ada's payments.
With so many transfers, she shows her account details and checks every alert in her bank app.
COUNTIF counts the rows that match. Ada finds 120 transfers, 70 cash and 30 POS, and checks they add to 220.
120 divided by 220, times 100, is about 54.5%. More than half her customers pay by transfer.
So she prints her account details clearly, and checks every alert in her bank app before releasing goods. A good summary leads to a decision.
Which sells most? Bar or column chart
Change over time? Line chart
Share of a whole? Pie, 2 to 5 slices only
Link between two measures? Scatter chart
Exact figures needed? A small table
Bars compare categories. Lines show change over time. For example, Ruth sells small chops in Port Harcourt. Her six weeks total 356,000 naira, a mean of about 59,333, so she uses a line chart.
Week 4 to Week 5 grew about 14.8%, then fell about 5.7%. She adds a note that Week 3 had heavy rain. Her title says what it shows: weekly sales trending up, Weeks 1 to 6, in naira.
Use a pie only for a few parts, and a table when someone needs exact numbers.
Read with care
Read every chart from the outside in. Sales 70 could mean 70 bottles or 70,000 naira, so check units. On a bar chart, the value axis should start at zero, otherwise small differences look huge.
Then show your chart to one person. If she cannot state the message in one sentence, improve it.
Key points
Remember
One row per record, one column per variable
Formulas start with = and update themselves
SUMIF adds by category; COUNTIF counts
Category totals must match the overall SUM
Bars compare, lines show time, pies stay small
To remember. Keep your table tidy. Let formulas do the work. Summarise by category and always check it adds up. And choose an honest chart with a clear title and units.

Why this matters
Numbers must be accurate and honest

Real data is rarely clean. People type quickly, two people record the same sale, a zero gets added by mistake. One wrong row can change a total or a decision.
Data can also be accurate but used badly: exposing private details, or pushing the reader to a wrong conclusion.
And many small businesses track only sales. In this module you learn the numbers that show whether you are really making money.
Find and fix
Common problems and their tools
Extra spaces and capitals: =PROPER(TRIM(B2))
Duplicates: a COUNTIF helper column
Blanks: =COUNTBLANK, then check receipts
Text numbers like 5k: retype as plain numbers
Typos: check =MAX and =MIN on every column
Jos North, jos north, and Jos North with two spaces become three groups in your summary. TRIM removes extra spaces and PROPER fixes the capitals.
A COUNTIF helper column shows TRUE for any receipt number that appears more than once.
COUNTBLANK tells you how many cells are empty. And numbers typed as text are left out of SUM.
Check the largest and smallest values. A 500,000 naira contribution in a group where most pay 5,000 needs checking against the receipt.

Two amounts were blank. The receipts show both members paid 5,000, so the total rises by 10,000.
One entry says 50,000, but the receipt says 5,000. She corrects it.
The new total is 562,000 naira, and it now matches the bank. She records every change in a cleaning log, so the executive can see what was corrected and why.
Prevent errors
Stop mistakes before they start
Keep the raw file untouched. Clean a copy.
Dropdowns for every category column
One shared form instead of mixed reports
Highlight suspicious values in red
Paste cleaned columns as values only
Keep a four-column cleaning log
Use Data validation to add a dropdown, such as Cash, Transfer and POS. People pick instead of typing, so spelling stays the same. Collect reports through one shared form.
Use conditional formatting to colour suspicious amounts. After cleaning with a formula, paste the clean column as values only.
Always keep the original raw file untouched, and keep a log: date, record, what was wrong, what you changed.
Protect people
Privacy before sharing
Counting who attended? You do not need home addresses.
Codes like P01 instead of names, no phone numbers, and no screenshots of member lists.
1 widow in Ward 3 may identify her. Combine small groups or report more broadly.
Ethical data work protects people. Collect only what you need, and say at the top of a survey what the answers are for.
Replace names with codes before sharing. A screenshot posted in a large WhatsApp group can be forwarded anywhere within minutes.
And watch very small groups, because a tiny number can point to one real person.
Who is missing from the survey?
48 of 120 members replied: a 40% response rate
36 of the 48 chose Saturday: 75%
Older members with basic phones were missing
Leaders collect the missing answers by phone
For example, a women's group in Enugu has 120 members. The coordinator sends a Google Forms link, and 48 reply. 36 of them choose Saturday for training.
But almost no older members replied, because many use basic phones without data. This is sampling bias.
So she reports: 75% of the 48 members who replied online prefer Saturday, and we are collecting the other answers before deciding.
Spot the trick
Misleading numbers to watch for
Cut-off axes that exaggerate change
Only the best months shown
Up 100% may mean from 2 to 4 orders
Averages that hide spread
Steady high returns promised: check SEC
Be suspicious of these. And remember, correlation is not causation. Zobo and fan sales rise together because of hot weather, not because one causes the other.
Promises of fixed, high monthly returns are a classic Ponzi warning sign. Check registration with the Securities and Exchange Commission Nigeria before paying.
Was Ada's September profitable?
For example, Ada checks her provisions shop's September receipts and expenses.
Revenue, 220 sales
Running costs
Illustrative figures. Total is net profit.
High sales do not guarantee profit. Ada's figures are illustrative.
Revenue minus cost of goods sold is gross profit: 110,000 naira. Divide by revenue and times 100, and her gross margin is 27.5%.
After 20,000 naira of running costs, her net profit is 90,000, a net margin of 22.5%.
If her supplier raises prices and she does not adjust, she will see it first in a falling gross margin.
Break-even
How many buckets must she sell?
Garri cost ₦2,000
Sells at ₦2,500
₦500 left from each bucket
Break-even: 40 buckets
Garri cost ₦2,200
Still sells at ₦2,500
Only ₦300 left from each
Break-even: about 67 buckets
Break-even is where you cover all costs. A trader has fixed costs of 20,000 naira a month. Each bucket of garri leaves 500 naira, so 20,000 divided by 500 is 40 buckets.
If the cost rises to 2,200, each bucket leaves only 300, and she needs about 67 buckets. That is why tracking costs matters as much as tracking sales.
Key points
Remember
Check totals, blanks, duplicates and extremes
Anonymise, and ask who could not respond
Correlation is a clue, not proof
Gross margin = gross profit ÷ revenue × 100
Track 3 to 5 KPIs weekly against targets
To remember. Clean before you count. Protect people and report honestly. And track 3 to 5 key numbers every week, including margin, not only sales.

The capstone
The five sheets of your workbook
Raw: the original records, never edited
Clean: consistent labels, no duplicates
Summary: SUMIF, COUNTIF, shares, metrics
Charts: two or three, each with a message title
Notes: question, dictionary, log, findings
Keep the original records untouched in Raw, and clean a copy.
Summarise and chart the clean data, with a message title on every chart.
In Notes, write your question and a data dictionary: each column's name, meaning, type and allowed values. It lets someone else check your work without asking you.
Do not invent records. The point is to practise on real, imperfect data.
Worked example
Ngozi's three-month workbook
For example, Ngozi runs a tailoring business in Nyanya, Abuja, and enters 84 orders.
July, 24 orders
August, 28 orders
September, 32 orders
Revenue by month, from SUMIF and COUNTIF.
Ngozi asks: is my business growing, and why are some customers unhappy? She removes 2 duplicate orders and fills missing delivery dates from her chats.
Revenue grows every month: about 23.8% from July to August, and about 21.2% to September.
In total, 785,000 naira. But COUNTIF shows 10 late orders out of 84, and 8 of the 10 were group aso ebi orders.

Before you submit
Accuracy and privacy checks
Cleaned rows and total explained in the log
Category totals add up to the overall total
Shares of a whole add up to 100%
Charts have titles, units, and zero axes
Codes, not names or phone numbers
Every column explained in the dictionary
Write no more than three findings, each with a number, and name what the data cannot show. Ngozi's data cannot show whether customers left because of lateness, so she plans to ask.
Then run these six checks before you submit.
Presenting
Lead with the answer, not the order you did the work.
Main message in one sentence
Two or three supporting numbers
A busy manager or donor will not read your spreadsheet. Start with the answer: we asked why deliveries were late, and the main reason is group orders.
Give two or three numbers and one chart. When speaking, round them: about one in eight orders, not 11.9 percent.
Then say what it means, and close with the decision you need, who will do what, and by when.
Outputs, outcomes and honesty
What you delivered: 45 enrolled, 38 completed, about 84.4%.
What changed: 25 of 38 keep weekly sales records, about 65.8%.
7 did not finish because of market days. So she asks to fund a Saturday cohort.
For example, a community programme in Ilorin trained women in bookkeeping. Outputs are what you delivered: 38 of 45 completed.
Outcomes are what changed. A phone follow-up three months later reached all 38, and 25 now keep weekly records. The donor headline: two in three graduates now keep weekly sales records.
She also reports the 7 who did not finish, and why. Funders usually notice missing numbers, and admitting limits increases trust.
For members, she sends one short WhatsApp message with the same facts and a clear next step.
Your 90-day plan
Vague goals or measurable targets
Record 100% of sales for 12 weeks
Margin from 24% to 26% by day 90
Repeat customer rate 50% by day 90
Grow my business cannot be checked. A target names the metric, the starting point, the goal and the date.

For example, Halima's kiosk earns about 95,000 naira a week at a 24% gross margin. In 90 days she will record every sale, raise margin to 26%, measure repeat customers, and test one change, such as a bulk-buy discount for two weeks.
Keep it to about three targets, and spend 30 minutes each week on your records and dashboard.
